newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenian PM confident of leading new government.
newsitem.headline: Slovenian PM confident of leading new government.

text.p: Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek said he expected his centre-left Liberal Democrats to emerge as the biggest party in a general election on Sunday, the second since independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.
But Drnovsek, 46, a former president of the Yugoslav federation between 1989 and 1990, declined to speculate on which parties he may invite to join his new administration.
"I expect...we will get the most support and the opportunity to form the next government," Drnovsek told reporters after voting near his home in central Ljubljana.

Drnovsek, a firm backer of European Union and NATO membership, is battling a loose rightist alliance, but will probably have to include one or two of the rightwing parties in a new government if he wants to push ahead with tough economic reforms to prepare Slovenia for EU entry by 2001.

Nearly 30 percent of Slovenia's 1.5 million voters had cast their ballots by 11 a.m. (1000 GMT) on a grey, rainy day. The figure was below the 33 percent recorded at the same time in the 1992 election when overall turnout was a high 85.8 percent.
The election for the 90-seat parliament was the second since Slovenia declared independence from Yugoslavia in June 1991 and a 10-day war against Yugoslav federal troops which left 64 people dead.

The mountainous republic's 3,534 polling stations opened at 7 a.m. local time (0600 GMT) and were due to close at 1800 GMT. An exit poll by Slovenia's main commercial television station POPtv was due to be released once polling ends.
Slovenian state television was scheduled to issue computer projections of the results by 1845 GMT. Final unofficial results were expected on Monday.
President Milan Kucan, the former Slovenian communist party chief who defied Belgrade's rule to lead his country to secession, was among the first to vote.
Kucan, speaking to reporters after casting his ballot near his modest home in Ljubjlana, said voters would support those parties committed to securing a stable future.
"They will support parties which are not just interested in arguing and looking back to the past, but those who have something to offer other than empty promises," he said.
Drnovsek managed to hold a fragile coalition together for the past four years to anchor a stable democracy and marshal one of the most prosperous economies among Europe's former communist states.
Moody's Investors Service in May gave Slovenia an A3 international credit rating, the same as the Czech Republic and ahead of Poland.

The economy has grown by an estimated 3.5 percent this year and inflation dropped to single-digit figures after a bout of hyperinflation in 1991-2, but the government has faced mounting criticism for a rising jobless rate, currently at 13.5 percent, and the sluggish pace of privatisation.

Drnovsek gave in to a series of public sector demands for higher pay this year. In an attempt to forestall further industrial action, Drnovsek has said economic belt-tightening in the next four years will be accompanied by tax cuts.
